stem: During one hemodialysis treatment, a nurse removes gloves after handling contaminated equipment and then prepares to care for the client's vascular access. Which action is required before touching the access?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene again before caring for the vascular access, even though gloves were worn for the previous task.
options.B: Skip hand hygiene because removing gloves eliminates microorganisms from the hands.
options.C: Use the same gloves again for vascular-access care if they are not visibly soiled.
options.D: Wait until the end of the dialysis session to perform hand hygiene because one episode per treatment is sufficient.

rationale: CDC dialysis guidance emphasizes hand hygiene as a core bloodstream-infection prevention practice and instructs patients to expect staff to clean their hands before and after caring for them or their vascular access. CDC intravascular-catheter guidance also requires hand hygiene before and after accessing or dressing vascular catheters, and glove use does not replace hand hygiene. Therefore, the nurse should perform hand hygiene again before access care. B, C, and D incorrectly treat glove removal or a single hand-hygiene episode as sufficient across separate contamination opportunities.
educational_objective: Perform hand hygiene at each indicated transition during dialysis care, including after glove removal and before vascular-access care, because gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Infections and Patients on Dialysis; Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention in the Dialysis Setting; Summary of Recommendations for Intravascular Catheter-Related Infection Prevention
source_version_date: Current CDC dialysis-safety and infection-control guidance accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: CDC 'Infections and Patients on Dialysis' → Steps to take: patients should make sure staff clean their hands before and after caring for them or their access. CDC 'Best Practices for Bloodstream Infection Prevention in the Dialysis Setting' → Core Interventions includes hand-hygiene observation and access-care asepsis. CDC intravascular-catheter recommendations → Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique: perform hand hygiene before and after accessing or dressing an intravascular catheter; glove use does not eliminate the need for hand hygiene.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports repeated hand hygiene at indicated points during dialysis/access care and establishes that gloves do not substitute for hand hygiene.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Hand Hygiene/Standard Precautions/Aseptic Technique: perform hand hygiene at appropriate times and prevent cross-contamination during vascular-access care.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand hygiene transitions during hemodialysis care
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's general rationale about 'multiple points of potential contamination' into an applied hand-hygiene decision with exact CDC support. The final item specifically tests that glove use/removal does not replace hand hygiene before a new vascular-access-care task.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Hand hygiene during hemodialysis vascular-access care
audit_findings.source_authority: Current official CDC dialysis-safety and intravascular-device infection-control guidance.
audit_findings.currentness: CDC's 2024 dialysis-safety pages and current intravascular-catheter recommendation pages remain active at the audit date.

claim_by_claim.stem: Transition from contaminated-equipment handling to vascular-access care creates a new hand-hygiene indication.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because CDC requires hand hygiene around access care and glove use does not replace it.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because hands can become contaminated during glove removal or through glove defects and hand hygiene remains required.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because contaminated/used gloves are not reused for a new clean or aseptic task.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because hand hygiene is performed at indicated moments throughout care, not once per treatment.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Avoids inventing a hand-rub duration or product requirement not needed by the item.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to hand hygiene across task transitions.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests glove-replaces-hand-hygiene misconception, C glove reuse, and D one-time-per-session thinking. Each is realistic and distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A is consistent with current hand-hygiene and access-care recommendations.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are immediate hand/glove actions at the same transition point and use parallel procedural wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control directly fits hand hygiene and prevention of cross-contamination.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited whether this duplicates Q1689. Q1689 tests hub antisepsis before catheter access; Q1696 tests hand hygiene despite prior glove use at a task transition. The infection-prevention constructs are distinct. No unresolved conflict remains.
